questions.title: M001 · Equality and Gini
questions.promptMarkdown: Everyone has the same positive income. What is the Gini coefficient on the 0–1 scale?
options: It depends on average income
hints: Start from the exact formula for the income ratio, growth rate, or average/marginal product of labour ($APL = Y/L$, $MPL = \Delta Y/\Delta L$).
Watch out for the classic trap: Higher Gini means more inequality, not more equality.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** 0

With equal income, the Lorenz curve coincides with the equality line. The gap is zero, so Gini is zero.
questions.pitfall: Higher Gini means more inequality, not more equality.

questions.title: M002 · Reading a Lorenz point
questions.promptMarkdown: A Lorenz curve contains (60%, 25%). What does this mean?
options: 60% of income goes to the poorest 25%.
Every person receives 25% of income.
The richest 60% receive 25% of total income.
The poorest 60% receive 25% of total income.
hints: Start from the exact formula for the income ratio, growth rate, or average/marginal product of labour ($APL = Y/L$, $MPL = \Delta Y/\Delta L$).
Watch out for the classic trap: Read population on x and income on y.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** The poorest 60% receive 25% of total income.

People are ranked from poorest to richest; both axes are cumulative shares.
questions.pitfall: Read population on x and income on y.

questions.promptMarkdown: All individual incomes rise by 8%, with nobody changing groups. What happens to the top-decile/bottom-decile average-income ratio?

It rises by 8%.

questions.title: M004 · Diminishing average product
questions.promptMarkdown: Farm output rises from 600 to 720 when labour rises from 10 to 15 workers. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Average output per worker rose.
Total output fell because average product fell.
Marginal product must be negative.
Total output rose, while average output per worker fell.
hints: Start from the exact formula for the income ratio, growth rate, or average/marginal product of labour ($APL = Y/L$, $MPL = \Delta Y/\Delta L$).
Watch out for the classic trap: Separate total output from output per worker.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** Total output rose, while average output per worker fell.

Average product changes from 60 to 48. Output still rises by 120, so lower average product does not imply falling total output.
questions.pitfall: Separate total output from output per worker.

questions.title: M005 · Average versus marginal product
questions.promptMarkdown: In a graph of total output Y against labour L, how do you identify average and marginal product at a point?
options: Both are the height Y.
Marginal product is always total output divided by labour.
Average product is the origin-to-point slope; marginal product is the tangent slope.
Average product is the tangent slope; marginal product is Y/L.
hints: Start from the exact formula for the income ratio, growth rate, or average/marginal product of labour ($APL = Y/L$, $MPL = \Delta Y/\Delta L$).
Watch out for the classic trap: A level, a ratio and a derivative are different quantities.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** Average product is the origin-to-point slope; marginal product is the tangent slope.

Average product is Y/L. Marginal product is the additional output from an additional unit of labour, represented by the local slope.
questions.pitfall: A level, a ratio and a derivative are different quantities.

questions.title: M006 · Institutions
questions.promptMarkdown: Which combination characterises the capitalist production system described in the course?
options: Only self-sufficient households with no trade.
All productive capital owned collectively by the state.
Private property, markets and firms.
No government, no regulation and no taxation.
hints: Start from the exact formula for the income ratio, growth rate, or average/marginal product of labour ($APL = Y/L$, $MPL = \Delta Y/\Delta L$).
Watch out for the classic trap: The presence of government does not by itself rule out capitalism.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** Private property, markets and firms.

Capitalism combines private ownership of productive assets, voluntary market exchange and production organised through firms.
questions.pitfall: The presence of government does not by itself rule out capitalism.

questions.title: M007 · GDP and wellbeing
questions.promptMarkdown: GDP rises after a costly pollution cleanup. Which statement is most defensible?
options: Cleanup services are never counted as production.
GDP automatically subtracts all environmental degradation.
Recorded production may rise even though environmental damage has reduced wellbeing.
The increase proves every citizen is better off.
hints: Start from the exact formula for the income ratio, growth rate, or average/marginal product of labour ($APL = Y/L$, $MPL = \Delta Y/\Delta L$).
Watch out for the classic trap: Higher measured GDP is not sufficient evidence of higher wellbeing.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** Recorded production may rise even though environmental damage has reduced wellbeing.

GDP measures production, not a complete account of welfare or natural-capital losses.
questions.pitfall: Higher measured GDP is not sufficient evidence of higher wellbeing.

questions.title: M008 · Equal cash transfer
questions.promptMarkdown: The top-decile average income is 900,000 NOK and the bottom-decile average is 100,000 NOK. Both rise by 50,000 NOK. What is the new ratio?
hints: Start from the exact formula for the income ratio, growth rate, or average/marginal product of labour ($APL = Y/L$, $MPL = \Delta Y/\Delta L$).
Watch out for the classic trap: Add the transfer to both numerator and denominator.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** 6.33

The new ratio is 950,000/150,000 = 6.33, below the original ratio of 9. The same cash transfer is a larger percentage gain for the poorer group.
questions.pitfall: Add the transfer to both numerator and denominator.

questions.title: M011 · Opportunity cost is net
questions.promptMarkdown: An afternoon café shift pays 700 NOK and effort costs the worker 200 NOK in money-equivalent terms. It is the best alternative to attending a lecture. What is the opportunity cost of attending?
options: 200 NOK
500 NOK
700 NOK
900 NOK
hints: Write down the total cost equation $C = wL + pR$ (slope $-w/p$) or separate direct cost from the net value of the next-best reservation option.
Watch out for the classic trap: Compare net benefits; wages alone can overstate the forgone alternative.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** 500 NOK

The best forgone alternative has net value 700−200 = 500.
questions.pitfall: Compare net benefits; wages alone can overstate the forgone alternative.

questions.title: M012 · Sunk ticket
questions.promptMarkdown: A non-refundable ticket bought last month cost 400 NOK. When deciding whether to attend tonight or work, how should the historical ticket payment enter the comparison?
options: It makes attending automatically optimal.
Treat it as sunk if it cannot be recovered under either choice.
Subtract it from the wage earned by working tonight.
Add it only to the cost of attending tonight.
hints: Write down the total cost equation $C = wL + pR$ (slope $-w/p$) or separate direct cost from the net value of the next-best reservation option.
Watch out for the classic trap: Check whether a cost changes with the decision.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** Treat it as sunk if it cannot be recovered under either choice.

The payment is the same past cost under both current alternatives. Current benefits and avoidable costs decide the choice.
questions.pitfall: Check whether a cost changes with the decision.

questions.title: M013 · Economic rent can be negative
questions.promptMarkdown: An activity gives net benefit 600 NOK; the best alternative gives 850 NOK. What is the economic rent from choosing the activity?
options: −250 NOK
600 NOK
250 NOK
hints: Write down the total cost equation $C = wL + pR$ (slope $-w/p$) or separate direct cost from the net value of the next-best reservation option.
Watch out for the classic trap: A negative rent means the alternative is better.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** −250 NOK

Rent is the chosen option’s net value minus the next-best option: 600−850 = −250.
questions.pitfall: A negative rent means the alternative is better.

questions.title: M014 · Dominance
questions.promptMarkdown: Two technologies produce the same output. A uses 3 labour hours and 7 energy units; B uses 4 hours and 8 units. Input prices are strictly positive. Which is correct?
options: A strictly dominates B.
Neither can dominate until prices are known.
B dominates A.
B is preferred because it uses more inputs.
hints: Write down the total cost equation $C = wL + pR$ (slope $-w/p$) or separate direct cost from the net value of the next-best reservation option.
Watch out for the classic trap: Dominance compares physical inputs while holding output fixed.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** A strictly dominates B.

A uses less of both costly inputs for identical output.
questions.pitfall: Dominance compares physical inputs while holding output fixed.

questions.title: M015 · Trade-off is not dominance
questions.promptMarkdown: For the same output, A uses (L=2,R=12), B uses (L=5,R=6). Which is correct?
options: B dominates because 6<12.
Add the two input quantities to decide the cheapest technology.
Neither dominates; cost depends on relative input prices.
A dominates because 2<5.
hints: Write down the total cost equation $C = wL + pR$ (slope $-w/p$) or separate direct cost from the net value of the next-best reservation option.
Watch out for the classic trap: Different input units cannot be added to establish dominance.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** Neither dominates; cost depends on relative input prices.

A saves labour while B saves energy. A common cost comparison requires wL+pR.
questions.pitfall: Different input units cannot be added to establish dominance.

questions.title: M016 · Isocost steepness
questions.promptMarkdown: Labour is on x and energy on y. The wage rises while the energy price stays fixed. What happens to the absolute isocost slope?
options: It stays fixed because output is fixed.
It rises because w/p rises.
It becomes positive.
It falls because p/w falls.
hints: Write down the total cost equation $C = wL + pR$ (slope $-w/p$) or separate direct cost from the net value of the next-best reservation option.
Watch out for the classic trap: Keep the axes fixed when interpreting a price change.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** It rises because w/p rises.

From R=C/p−(w/p)L, slope is −w/p. A higher wage makes it more negative and steeper.
questions.pitfall: Keep the axes fixed when interpreting a price change.

questions.title: M017 · Carbon price and choice
questions.promptMarkdown: A tax increases the price of diesel relative to electricity. For a given transport output, what incentive does this create?
options: An incentive to use a less diesel-intensive technology when its new cost is lower.
Diesel-intensive technology becomes cheaper.
There is no effect because physical input requirements do not change.
Every firm must immediately use zero diesel whatever its costs.
hints: Write down the total cost equation $C = wL + pR$ (slope $-w/p$) or separate direct cost from the net value of the next-best reservation option.
Watch out for the classic trap: An incentive is not a guarantee that every firm switches.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** An incentive to use a less diesel-intensive technology when its new cost is lower.

The tax changes relative input costs and can reverse the ranking of undominated technologies.
questions.pitfall: An incentive is not a guarantee that every firm switches.

questions.title: M018 · Innovation and competitors
questions.promptMarkdown: An innovator initially earns extra profit from a cheaper process. Other firms later adopt it. Why can the innovation rent shrink?
options: Competition and diffusion erode the initial cost advantage.
The original innovation ceases to reduce costs physically.
Adoption by rivals gives the original firm permanent exclusive rights.
Opportunity cost always becomes zero after one year.
hints: Write down the total cost equation $C = wL + pR$ (slope $-w/p$) or separate direct cost from the net value of the next-best reservation option.
Watch out for the classic trap: A successful invention need not generate permanent extra profit.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** Competition and diffusion erode the initial cost advantage.

Innovation rents can be temporary as rivals copy/adopt and prices adjust.
questions.pitfall: A successful invention need not generate permanent extra profit.

questions.title: M019 · Isocost slope
questions.promptMarkdown: For C=300L+150R, labour is on x and energy on y. What is the slope of an isocost line?

questions.title: M021 · Innovation rent
questions.promptMarkdown: For identical output and equal revenues, the old process costs 4,600 NOK and the new one costs 3,850 NOK. Adoption has no additional costs. What is the extra profit per batch?

questions.title: M022 · Isocost intercept
questions.promptMarkdown: A firm has an input-cost budget of 6,000 NOK. Energy costs 200 NOK/unit. What is the energy-axis intercept, at L=0?

30 energy units
6,000 energy units
200 energy units

questions.title: M023 · Price threshold
questions.promptMarkdown: A=(L=4,R=10) and B=(L=7,R=4) produce the same output. Energy costs 100 NOK/unit. At which wage do their costs match?
options: 600 NOK/hour
200 NOK/hour
100 NOK/hour
300 NOK/hour

**Correct Answer:** 200 NOK/hour

4w+1,000 = 7w+400, so 600=3w and w=200. Above this wage, labour-saving A is cheaper.

questions.promptMarkdown: Studying has net benefit 800 NOK and working has net benefit 650 NOK. A grant of 100 NOK is paid regardless of the afternoon choice. What happens to the rent from studying?

It stays 150 NOK.

questions.title: M025 · Same utility
questions.promptMarkdown: B and C lie on one indifference curve. B has more consumption and less free time than C. What follows?
options: The person is equally satisfied with B and C.
B and C must have identical coordinates.
B must be preferred because consumption is larger.
C must be preferred because free time is larger.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Watch out for the classic trap: Equal utility does not mean equal quantities.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** The person is equally satisfied with B and C.

An indifference curve joins equally preferred bundles. Changes in the two goods compensate each other.
questions.pitfall: Equal utility does not mean equal quantities.

questions.title: M026 · No crossing
questions.promptMarkdown: Why can two distinct standard indifference curves for two desirable goods not cross?
options: Because all indifference curves must be straight.
Because consumption must be identical on every curve.
Because budget lines cannot cross.
A common point would imply equal utility on both, conflicting with preference for a bundle with more of one good and no less of the other.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Watch out for the classic trap: This concerns consistent preferences, not a particular wage.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** A common point would imply equal utility on both, conflicting with preference for a bundle with more of one good and no less of the other.

Indifference is transitive. Crossing would make two bundles equally preferred even when one strictly dominates the other.
questions.pitfall: This concerns consistent preferences, not a particular wage.

questions.title: M027 · Meaning of MRS
questions.promptMarkdown: Free time is on x and consumption on y. What does MRS measure?
options: Minimum consumption needed to survive.
Consumption the market forces the person to sacrifice per hour.
Total utility divided by working hours.
Consumption the person is locally willing to give up per extra hour of free time at constant utility.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Watch out for the classic trap: MRT describes the available market trade-off.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** Consumption the person is locally willing to give up per extra hour of free time at constant utility.

MRS is the magnitude of the indifference-curve slope. It describes preferences at the current bundle.
questions.pitfall: MRT describes the available market trade-off.

questions.title: M028 · Point versus interval
questions.promptMarkdown: Consumption falls by 100 when free time rises by 2 hours along an indifference curve. What is established?
options: The exact derivative at both endpoints is necessarily −50.
Utility fell by 100.
The average trade-off over that interval is 50 consumption units per hour.
The MRS is 100 hours per consumption unit.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Watch out for the classic trap: A table interval does not identify every tangent slope.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** The average trade-off over that interval is 50 consumption units per hour.

The secant slope is −100/2=−50. A local derivative requires additional information.
questions.pitfall: A table interval does not identify every tangent slope.

questions.title: M029 · Diminishing MRS
questions.promptMarkdown: Along a standard convex indifference curve, moving toward more free time and less consumption usually does what?
options: Makes MRS rise without limit.
Makes the budget wage fall automatically.
Raises utility along the same curve.
Reduces willingness to sacrifice consumption for another small increase in free time.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Watch out for the classic trap: Do not confuse moving along preferences with changing market wages.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** Reduces willingness to sacrifice consumption for another small increase in free time.

When free time becomes more abundant relative to consumption, the marginal willingness to exchange consumption for it falls.
questions.pitfall: Do not confuse moving along preferences with changing market wages.

questions.title: M030 · Budget line meaning
questions.promptMarkdown: At a given amount of free time, what does the consumption level on the budget line represent?
options: The person’s utility score.
The amount the government guarantees regardless of work.
Minimum required earnings for happiness.
Maximum affordable consumption under the stated income assumptions.

Markets allow voluntary exchange, so people can specialise in producing some goods while consuming many others. Firms coordinate inputs and people in production. questions.title: S008 · Economic rent and sunk expenditure
questions.promptMarkdown:
A festival ticket bought earlier cost 500 NOK and cannot be resold or refunded. Attending gives enjoyment 900 and discomfort cost 200. Working instead gives wages 800 and effort cost 250. Explain the current decision and rent from attending.

questions.solutionMarkdown: The historical ticket payment is sunk: it is unrecoverable under both current options. Attending has current net value 900−200=700. Working has net value 800−250=550, the best forgone alternative. Attending therefore has rent 700−550=150 NOK and is preferred under these assumptions. Counting the old payment only against attending would incorrectly make the decision depend on a cost that can no longer change.

questions.title: S009 · Indifference curves and MRS
questions.promptMarkdown:
Explain an indifference curve for consumption and free time. Explain why MRS can change along one curve even though utility is constant.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Define equal utility along one curve.
Define MRS with axes and units.
Explain diminishing MRS without claiming utility changes.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Make sure your concise answer covers: Define equal utility along one curve; Define MRS with axes and units.
questions.solutionMarkdown: An indifference curve joins bundles giving the same utility. Moving along it changes the mix of consumption and free time while preserving overall satisfaction. MRS is the local consumption sacrifice per extra free hour that preserves utility, equal to the magnitude of the curve’s slope. With standard convex preferences, more free time and less consumption reduce willingness to sacrifice still more consumption, so MRS falls. Constant total utility does not imply a constant marginal trade-off.

questions.title: S010 · Budget and willingness
questions.promptMarkdown:
A worker keeps 240 NOK/hour, receives 160 NOK/day independently of work and has 16 free hours out of 24. Find maximum consumption and MRT. At this bundle MRS is 360 NOK/hour. Explain a beneficial local adjustment.

*(Maximum 200 words)*

hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Make sure your concise answer covers: Correct work hours and consumption; Correct MRT and its economic meaning.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Work is 24−16=8 hours, so maximum consumption is 240×8+160=2,080 NOK. MRT is the net hourly wage, 240 NOK/hour; the budget slope is −240. MRS of 360 exceeds MRT, so the worker values a small increase in free time more than the consumption it costs. Moving toward more free time and less work can increase utility, under standard smooth preferences. The information establishes a direction, not the exact new optimum.

questions.title: S011 · Transfer versus wage tax cut
questions.promptMarkdown:
Compare an unconditional daily transfer with a cut in a constant wage-income tax rate. Explain budget shape, MRT and effects on work, assuming free time is a normal good.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Transfer: parallel shift and unchanged MRT.
Tax cut: net wage/MRT rise and rotation.

hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Make sure your concise answer covers: Transfer: parallel shift and unchanged MRT; Tax cut: net wage/MRT rise and rotation.
questions.solutionMarkdown: A transfer raises non-labour income and shifts the budget line upward in parallel, leaving the net wage and MRT unchanged. Its income effect encourages more leisure and less work under the normal-good assumption. A wage tax cut raises the net hourly wage and makes the line steeper, pivoting around the zero-work bundle when other income is fixed. It creates an income effect toward more leisure and a substitution effect toward less leisure. Their relative sizes determine the final change in work. Preferences themselves need not change.

questions.promptMarkdown:
Hourly wage is 210 NOK, effort disutility 30, benefit 75 and unemployment stigma 15, all hourly equivalents. Normal work is 32 hours/week; an identical job would be found after 25 weeks. Calculate rent per hour and the total loss from dismissal.

questions.promptMarkdown:
A model gives weekly fallback r=6,000, effort cost c=1,500, horizon h=50 weeks and detection time s=10. Formula supplied: w_NS=r+c+[s/(h−s)]c. Calculate the wage and explain why later detection raises it.

Delayed detection increases the time earning wages without effort and reduces the remaining time suffering dismissal within the fixed horizon. questions.title: S015 · Incomplete contracts and unemployment
questions.promptMarkdown:
Explain why imperfect observation of effort can lead a firm to pay above the outside option. Explain why higher unemployment changes the wage needed for effort.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Explain observability/enforcement problem.
Connect above-fallback pay and job-loss cost.

hints: Separate net hourly value when employed ($w - c$) from net hourly value when unemployed ($b - s$), and multiply only over expected unemployment duration.
Make sure your concise answer covers: Explain observability/enforcement problem; Connect above-fallback pay and job-loss cost.
questions.solutionMarkdown: A contract cannot fully specify or enforce every aspect of effort. A worker needs something to lose from dismissal, so the job must provide a net advantage over the next-best alternative. This employment rent helps motivate effort. Higher unemployment generally makes a comparable replacement job harder to obtain, increasing the expected cost of dismissal at a given wage. A firm can then maintain effort at a lower required wage, other things equal. This is a mechanism within the model, not a claim that the employer knows each outside option perfectly.

questions.title: S017 · Why supply follows MC
questions.promptMarkdown:
Explain why a price-taking firm with increasing marginal cost chooses an interior operating output where P=MC. Does this imply that profit is zero?

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Explain marginal revenue for a price taker.
Compare P and MC on both sides.
Distinguish marginal condition from total profit.
hints: Check whether the shock changes buyers' WTP (shifts Demand), sellers' marginal cost (shifts Supply), or merely moves along an unchanged curve.
Make sure your concise answer covers: Explain marginal revenue for a price taker; Compare P and MC on both sides.
questions.solutionMarkdown: A price taker earns the market price on each additional unit. While price exceeds marginal cost, an extra unit adds more revenue than cost, so expanding increases profit. Beyond the point where MC exceeds price, further output reduces profit. Thus the interior operating optimum is P=MC under the stated conditions. Profit need not be zero because total profit depends on average total costs and fixed costs, not only the cost of the marginal unit.

questions.title: S018 · A demand increase and cheaper production
questions.promptMarkdown:
A normal good becomes more popular while a production innovation lowers marginal cost. Use supply and demand to explain what can and cannot be concluded about equilibrium price and quantity.

*(Maximum 200 words)*

Their effects on price oppose: the demand increase raises it and the supply increase lowers it. Without the sizes of the shifts, the final price direction is ambiguous. A price change caused by these shocks represents movement along a curve, while the underlying preference and technology changes shift curves.

questions.title: S019 · Ceiling and shortage
questions.promptMarkdown:
Demand is Qd=120−2P and supply is Qs=2P. Calculate the competitive equilibrium. A ceiling of P=20 is imposed. Calculate the shortage and explain why the market does not clear.

Demand is P=120−Q and supply before a per-unit tariff is P=20+Q. A tariff of 20 shifts supply to P=40+Q. Find the old and new equilibria and explain who bears the price wedge.

questions.promptMarkdown:
Employment is above N*, so WS lies above PS. Explain the wage–price process and why a higher nominal wage alone need not solve the conflict.

*(Maximum 200 words)*

questions.promptMarkdown:
A translator keeps 300 NOK/hour, has no other income and spends all earnings on daily consumption. The day has 24 hours. In the supplied diagram B=(12,3,600), E=(16,2,400) and D=(20,1,200). The green curve is tangent at E; the orange curve passes through B and D. Both goods are desirable.

- **b)** At B, the orange indifference curve is steeper than the budget line. Explain a utility-improving local change. *(3 marks)*
- **c)** Why are B and D equally preferred in the diagram, while E is preferred to both? *(2 marks)*
- **d)** At D, MRS is below MRT. Explain the adjustment and the tangency condition at E. Does tangency apply automatically at all endpoint choices? *(3 marks)*

a) Correct MRT and work-hour calculations.
b) Interpret steepness as MRS>MRT.
b) Explain willingness versus market cost.
b) Give correct direction and utility implication.

c) Explain higher affordable utility at E.

questions.solutionMarkdown:
- **a)** x is free time t; y is consumption c. The budget is c=300(24−t), with slope −300 and MRT=300 NOK/hour. B means 12 hours of work; E means 8. Points below the line are affordable; above it are not.
- **b)** MRS is greater than 300 at B. The translator values an extra small amount of leisure more than its market opportunity cost. Moving right along the budget line toward more leisure and less work can raise utility. B being affordable does not establish optimality.
- **c)** B and D lie on the same orange indifference curve and give the same utility despite different quantities. E is on the higher green curve. It is affordable and reaches a higher utility level; geometric distance from the origin is not the criterion.
- **d)** At D an extra free hour costs more than the person values it, so working a little more can improve utility. At E the marginal willingness and feasible trade-off match: MRS=MRT=300. This is the standard smooth interior optimum; an optimum at a time-endowment boundary need not satisfy equal slopes.

questions.promptMarkdown:

- **b)** Using the diagram’s E→G→F convention, calculate income, substitution and total changes in free time. *(3 marks)*
- **c)** Why does equal utility at F and G not mean they have equal MRS? *(2 marks)*
- **d)** Explain why this does not prove every wage rise reduces work. What is the role of the hypothetical 1,740 NOK? *(3 marks)*

a) Both consumption checks.
b) Correct +3.9.
b) Correct −2.9 and +1.

c) Separate utility level from local slope.
c) Correct MRS values from the two tangent slopes.

Structure your multi-part answer step by step: Correct opportunity-cost/pivot explanation; Correct +3.9; Separate utility level from local slope.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
- **a)** An extra free hour now costs 600 rather than 300 in forgone earnings. The line pivots around (24,0). Old E has 8×300=2,400 and new F has 7×600=4,200.
- **b)** Income effect:19.9−16=+3.9 hours. Substitution effect:17−19.9=−2.9. Total:+1 hour, equal to F−E. G is hypothetical and is not a third observed actual choice.
- **c)** They are different bundles on one indifference curve. Utility is constant along it, but its slope can vary. At F, tangency to the actual new line gives MRS=600; at G, tangency to the old-slope hypothetical line gives MRS=300.
- **d)** For normal leisure, greater purchasing power encourages more free time while the higher opportunity cost encourages less. In this example the income effect dominates, but another preference pattern could reverse the net change. The 1,740 is hypothetical non-labour income shifting the old-slope line in parallel; it is not added to the hourly wage. This is a utility-compensated graphical decomposition.

questions.title: C008 · Benefits and equilibrium unemployment
questions.promptMarkdown:
The supplied WS–PS diagram measures employment N as a percentage of working-age population and real wage on y. Labour force L=90, productivity λ=100 and price-setting real wage=60. Initial employment N*=80. After a benefit increase, the new WS intersects the same PS at N=75. Treat all stated population quantities as the same units.

- **a)** Calculate initial employment, participation and unemployment rates. Explain their denominators. *(2 marks)*
- **b)** Explain why WS slopes up and why higher benefits shift it rather than merely causing movement along it. *(3 marks)*
- **c)** Find the new unemployment rate and explain why real wage stays 60. *(2 marks)*
- **d)** Explain why lower wage offers from unemployed applicants do not automatically eliminate the original unemployment. *(3 marks)*

questions.solutionMarkdown:
- **a)** Employment rate=80%; participation=90%. The unemployed are 90−80=10 percentage points of population. Their share of the labour force is 10/90≈11.11%. The remaining 10% of population are outside the labour force.
- **b)** At higher employment, comparable replacement jobs are easier to find, reducing dismissal costs at a fixed wage. Higher pay is then needed for effort. Benefits are a background determinant: raising them improves the fallback at every N, so the whole WS shifts up. A change in N alone would be movement along a fixed WS.
- **c)** Unemployment becomes 90−75=15 population points, or 15/90≈16.67% of labour force. PS remains at 60 because productivity and pricing are unchanged. The new intersection is leftward, at the same height.
- **d)** The model requires a wage high enough to motivate effort after hiring, not only one an applicant accepts. Cutting wages reduces the rent lost on dismissal and can make shirking attractive. An island has domestic fish producers selling 24 million NOK to restaurants and domestic electricity producers selling 6 million to restaurants. - **b)** What are exports from these transactions? If C=30, I=10 and G=5 million with this GDP and X, calculate imports. *(3 marks)*
- **c)** Explain how a forward-looking household’s response differs for temporary and permanent future income losses. *(2 marks)*

questions.title: Exam-Calibrated Q1 · Inequality & Production Functions
questions.promptMarkdown: In a country, the richest $10\%$ of the population has an average annual income of $1,200,000\text{ NOK}$, while the poorest $10\%$ has an average annual income of $150,000\text{ NOK}$. Suppose every inhabitant in both groups receives an unconditional cash transfer of $+30,000\text{ NOK}$. Which statement is **correct**?
options: The rich/poor ratio remains unchanged at $8.0$ because both groups received the exact same amount in kroner.
The rich/poor ratio decreases from $8.0$ to $6.83$.
The rich/poor ratio increases because the absolute income gap in kroner increases.
The rich/poor ratio only changes if both groups' incomes grow by the same percentage.
hints: Start from the exact formula for the income ratio, growth rate, or average/marginal product of labour ($APL = Y/L$, $MPL = \Delta Y/\Delta L$).
Watch out for the classic trap: Equal cash transfers in kroner give a larger percentage boost to the poor (lowering the 90/10 ratio), whereas equal percentage growth leaves the ratio unchanged.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Option: B)**
- **Initial rich/poor ratio**: $\frac{1,200,000}{150,000} = \mathbf{8.0}$.
- **After adding $+30,000\text{ NOK}$ to both**: $\frac{1,230,000}{180,000} = \mathbf{6.833} < 8.0$.
- **Why**: Adding an equal absolute amount in kroner represents a $+20\%$ increase for the poorest $10\%$ ($30\text{k}/150\text{k}$) vs. only $+2.5\%$ for the richest $10\%$ ($30\text{k}/1,200\text{k}$), lowering the ratio. (Equal *percentage* changes leave the ratio unchanged.)

questions.promptMarkdown: A firm uses labour ($L$, horizontal axis, wage $w = 400\text{ NOK/hour}$) and energy ($R$, vertical axis, price $p = 200\text{ NOK/unit}$). Which statement about the firm's isocost lines is **correct**?

The slope of the isocost lines is $-2.0$, and Technologies $A(4, 10)$ and $B(6, 6)$ lie on the same isocost line with total cost $3,600\text{ NOK}$.

questions.title: Exam-Calibrated Q3 · Optimal Choice: $MRS$ vs. $MRT$
questions.promptMarkdown: A worker with hourly wage $w = 300\text{ NOK/hour}$ is currently choosing $14\text{ hours}$ of free time ($10\text{ hours}$ of work) and $3,000\text{ NOK}$ of consumption. At this bundle, her Marginal Rate of Substitution ($MRS$) between free time and consumption is $450\text{ NOK}$. To maximize her utility, what should she do?
options: Keep working $10\text{ hours}$, because $3,000 / 10 = 300 = w$.
Work more hours (reduce free time), because $MRS > MRT$.
Work fewer hours (increase free time), because she values an extra hour of free time ($450\text{ NOK}$) at more than its market opportunity cost ($MRT = 300\text{ NOK}$).
Work more hours, because the substitution effect always dominates when $MRS = 450$.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Watch out for the classic trap: When $MRS > MRT$, the worker values an extra hour of free time above the hourly wage $w$, so utility rises by working fewer hours (more free time).
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Option: C)**
- At $(t=14, c=3000)$, $MRS = 450 > MRT = w = 300$. She is willing to give up $450\text{ NOK}$ of consumption to gain $1\text{ hour}$ of free time, whereas the market only requires her to give up $300\text{ NOK}$ in wage income. Moving right along the budget line (**more free time, less work**) increases her utility until $MRS$ falls to $300$.
questions.pitfall: When $MRS > MRT$, the worker values an extra hour of free time above the hourly wage $w$, so utility rises by working fewer hours (more free time).

questions.promptMarkdown: In an economy with a working-age population of $2,000,000$, there are $1,300,000$ employed workers and $100,000$ unemployed workers. Suppose $100,000$ previously inactive students graduate and enter the labour force: $60,000$ immediately start jobs and $40,000$ are actively searching for work. Your best alternative use of Saturday afternoon is working an extra shift at a café, which pays $800\text{ NOK}$ in wages and has an effort disutility of $250\text{ NOK}$.
1. What is the **opportunity cost** and the **economic cost** of attending the concert?
2. What is the **economic rent** of attending the concert, and should you go?
rubricChecks: Compute net value of concert (900 - 150 = 750 NOK) and café reservation option (800 - 250 = 550 NOK)
State opportunity cost (550 NOK) and economic cost (150 + 550 = 700 NOK)
Calculate positive economic rent (+200 NOK) and conclude to attend
hints: Write down the total cost equation $C = wL + pR$ (slope $-w/p$) or separate direct cost from the net value of the next-best reservation option.
Watch out for the classic trap: Opportunity cost is the net value (benefit minus effort cost) of the best foregone alternative, never the gross wage alone.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
1. **Net value of each option**:
   - **Concert (chosen option A)**: $\text{Benefit } (900\text{ NOK}) - \text{Direct discomfort cost } (150\text{ NOK}) = \mathbf{750\text{ NOK}}$.
   - **Working at the café (reservation option B)**: $\text{Wage } (800\text{ NOK}) - \text{Effort disutility } (250\text{ NOK}) = \mathbf{550\text{ NOK}}$.
   - The **opportunity cost** of attending the concert is the net value of the best foregone alternative (working at the café): **$550\text{ NOK}$**.
   - The **economic cost** of attending the concert is the sum of its direct cost and opportunity cost: $150\text{ NOK} + 550\text{ NOK} = \mathbf{700\text{ NOK}}$.
2. **Economic rent and decision**:
   $$\text{Economic Rent} = \text{Net Value}(\text{Concert}) - \text{Opportunity Cost} = 750 - 550 = \mathbf{200\text{ NOK}} \quad (= 900 - 700)$$
   Because the economic rent is strictly positive ($+200\text{ NOK} > 0$), **yes, you should attend the concert**.
questions.pitfall: Opportunity cost is the net value (benefit minus effort cost) of the best foregone alternative, never the gross wage alone.

questions.title: Exam-Calibrated Q8 · Numerical Employment Rent & No-Shirking Wage (`Fall 2025` / `V2026` / `Lecture 11` Style
questions.promptMarkdown:
Sofia works $37.5\text{ hours per week}$ at an hourly wage of $160\text{ NOK/hour}$. Her disutility of work effort is $25\text{ NOK/hour}$. If she loses her job, she receives unemployment benefits of $65\text{ NOK/hour}$ and experiences a psychological cost of being unemployed equal to $15\text{ NOK/hour}$. She evaluates her situation over a $120\text{-week}$ horizon and expects it to take **$32\text{ weeks}$** to find a new, identical job.
1. Calculate Sofia's **employment rent per hour** and her **total employment rent**.
2. Suppose instead that we measure payoffs weekly: Sofia's weekly reservation wage is $w_r = 6,000\text{ NOK}$, weekly effort cost is $c = 1,200\text{ NOK}$, her planning horizon is $h = 80\text{ weeks}$, and a shirking worker is caught and fired after $s = 20\text{ weeks}$. Calculate the firm's minimum **no-shirking weekly wage $w^{NS}$**.
rubricChecks: Compute net hourly employed value (135 NOK/h), unemployed value (50 NOK/h), and hourly rent (85 NOK/h)
Multiply by expected unemployment hours (37.5 * 32 = 1,200 h) to get 102,000 NOK total employment rent
Equate shirking gain (c*s) to lost rent to find no-shirking weekly wage w^NS = 7,600 NOK/week
hints: Separate net hourly value when employed ($w - c$) from net hourly value when unemployed ($b - s$), and multiply only over expected unemployment duration.
Watch out for the classic trap: Multiply hourly employment rent only by expected hours of unemployment ($37.5 \times 32$), not the entire 120-week planning horizon.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
1. **Sofia's Employment Rent**:
   - **Net hourly value when employed**: $w - c = 160 - 25 = \mathbf{135\text{ NOK/hour}}$.
   - **Net hourly value when unemployed**: $b - s = 65 - 15 = \mathbf{50\text{ NOK/hour}}$.
   - **Employment rent per hour**: $135 - 50 = \mathbf{85\text{ NOK/hour}}$.
   - **Expected hours of unemployment**: $37.5\text{ hours/week} \times 32\text{ weeks} = \mathbf{1,200\text{ hours}}$ *(weeks 33–120 are identical in both states and do not affect the cost of job loss)*.
   - **Total Employment Rent**: $85\text{ NOK/hour} \times 1,200\text{ hours} = \mathbf{102,000\text{ NOK}}$.
2. **Minimum No-Shirking Weekly Wage ($w^{NS}$)**:
   Equating the effort cost saved during the $s = 20$ weeks of shirking ($\text{Area A} = c \cdot s$) with the employment rent lost during the remaining $h - s = 60$ weeks ($\text{Area B} = (w - c - w_r)(h - s)$):
   $$w^{NS} = w_r + c + \left(\frac{s}{h - s}\right)c = 6,000 + 1,200 + \left(\frac{20}{80 - 20}\right)(1,200) = 7,200 + 400 = \mathbf{7,600\text{ NOK/week}}$$
questions.pitfall: Multiply hourly employment rent only by expected hours of unemployment ($37.5 \times 32$), not the entire 120-week planning horizon.

questions.title: Exam-Calibrated Q9 · Value-Added GDP & Two Recession Definitions (`Topic 8 Ex. 1–3` Style
questions.promptMarkdown:
In a small island economy with no government ($G=0$), fisherfolk catch fish worth $20\text{ million NOK}$ using $0$ intermediate inputs and sell all the fish to local restaurants. The restaurants buy $20\text{ million NOK}$ of fish and $5\text{ million NOK}$ of electricity (produced domestically with $0$ inputs) and sell meals worth $70\text{ million NOK}$ exclusively to foreign cruise tourists.
1. Calculate the economy's **GDP** using the value-added method and state the size of **Exports ($X$)**.
2. Suppose a volcanic eruption permanently destroys half of the island's fishing grounds, permanently lowering the economy's output level by $30\%$. Is the island in a permanent recession under **Definition 1** and **Definition 2** of a recession?
rubricChecks: Sum sector value added (20 + 5 + 45 = 70 million NOK GDP) and identify Exports X = 70 million NOK
Evaluate Definition 1 (recession only while output is actively falling during transition)
Evaluate Definition 2 (not a permanent recession because potential/normal capacity permanently fell)
hints: Avoid double-counting intermediate inputs in GDP, check both recession definitions (falling output vs. below potential), and test credit/behavioral limits to smoothing.
Watch out for the classic trap: Subtract intermediate fish and electricity inputs from restaurant sales to avoid double counting, and note a permanent capacity loss resets 'normal' output.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
1. **Value-Added GDP and Exports**:
   - **Fisherfolk value added**: $20 - 0 = 20\text{ mill. NOK}$.
   - **Electricity value added**: $5 - 0 = 5\text{ mill. NOK}$.
   - **Restaurants value added**: $70 - (20 + 5) = 45\text{ mill. NOK}$.
   - **Total GDP**: $\sum \text{Value Added} = 20 + 5 + 45 = \mathbf{70\text{ million NOK}}$ (which equals the market value of final meals sold to end-users, avoiding double counting of fish and electricity).
   - Because all meals are sold to foreign tourists, **Exports $X = \mathbf{70\text{ million NOK}}$**.
2. **Recession Definitions**:
   - **Definition 1 (Output is declining / negative growth)**: The economy is in a recession **only during the transition period while GDP is actively falling** by $30\%$; once output stabilizes at the lower level, the recession is over.
   - **Definition 2 (Output is below its normal/potential level)**: **No**, it is not a permanent recession because the volcanic eruption permanently reduced the island's productive capacity—the $30\%$ lower output is the economy's **"new normal"**.
questions.pitfall: Subtract intermediate fish and electricity inputs from restaurant sales to avoid double counting, and note a permanent capacity loss resets 'normal' output.

questions.title: Exam-Calibrated Q10 · Conflicting Claims & the Wage–Price Spiral (`V2026 Exam Part 2 Q3` Style
questions.promptMarkdown: Using the wage-setting and price-setting (WS–PS) model, explain how **persistent inflation** can arise from **conflicting claims on output** when aggregate demand is high and unemployment is low, and explain how an increase in unemployment dampens inflation. *(Max 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Define PS real wage w^PS = lambda(1 - sigma) and upward-sloping WS curve
Explain positive bargaining gap (w^WS > w^PS) when N > N* and resulting nominal wage-price spiral
Explain how higher unemployment raises cost of job loss and dampens nominal wage demands
hints: Compare the real wage required for effort ($w^{WS}$) with the price-setting real wage ($w^{PS}$) to see whether a positive bargaining gap drives a wage–price spiral.
Watch out for the classic trap: At low unemployment ($N > N^*$), $w^{WS} > w^{PS}$ creates conflicting claims exceeding $\lambda$, driving alternating $W \uparrow$ and $P \uparrow$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
In the WS–PS model, each worker produces $\lambda$ units of output, which is divided between the worker's real wage ($w$) and the firm's profit per worker ($\lambda - w$). The horizontal **PS curve** represents the real wage $w^{PS} = \lambda(1-\sigma)$ consistent with firms' profit-maximizing price markup $\sigma$, while the upward-sloping **WS curve** shows the real wage $w^{WS}$ needed to motivate workers at each employment level.

When aggregate demand is high and unemployment is low ($N > N^*$), the WS curve lies **above** the PS curve ($w^{WS} > w^{PS}$). There are **conflicting claims**: workers' real wage demands plus firms' target profit share exceed $100\%$ of output per worker $\lambda$ (a positive **bargaining gap**). Low unemployment reduces the cost of job loss, forcing firms to raise **nominal wages ($W \uparrow$)** to recruit and retain workers. Higher wage costs squeeze profit margins, so firms respond by raising **prices ($P \uparrow$)** to restore their markup $\sigma$. This erodes the real wage back to $w^{PS}$, triggering a continuous **wage–price spiral**.

Higher unemployment increases workers' fear of job loss (employment rent), weakening nominal wage demands and shrinking the bargaining gap, which slows cost and price growth (**disinflation**).
questions.pitfall: At low unemployment ($N > N^*$), $w^{WS} > w^{PS}$ creates conflicting claims exceeding $\lambda$, driving alternating $W \uparrow$ and $P \uparrow$.

questions.title: Exam-Calibrated Q11 · The WS–PS Model, Trade Unions, Norwegian *Frontfag* & Lorenz Inequality (`Fall 2024` + `Fall 2025` + `Lecture 13` Synthesis
questions.promptMarkdown:
Consider the macroeconomic WS–PS diagram where the horizontal axis measures Employment $N$ (with a vertical line at the Labour Force $L = 90\%$) and the vertical axis measures the Real Wage $w = W/P$ (with a horizontal dashed line at output per worker $\lambda = 100$ and a horizontal Price-Setting curve at $w^{PS} = 60$). The Wage-Setting curve $WS_0$ intersects $PS$ at **Point A** ($N^* = 80\%, w^* = 60$).
- **a)** Define the **labour force** and explain why the wage-setting ($WS$) curve is upward-sloping.
- **b)** Explain why **Point A** is the equilibrium in the labour market, and explain why firms do not cut the wage below $w^* = 60$ even though $10\%$ of the working-age population ($10$ out of $90$ in the labour force) is unemployed.
- **c)** Distinguish between a trade union's **bargaining (strike-threat) effect** and its **voice (motivation) effect** in the WS–PS diagram. How can the **Norwegian model of coordinated wage formation (*frontfagsmodellen*)** be illustrated in this diagram, and does it lead to a higher equilibrium real wage?
- **d)** Suppose new competing firms enter the product market, reducing firms' profit markup $\sigma$ from $0.40$ to $0.30$. Explain how this affects the WS–PS equilibrium.
- **e)** Show how the initial equilibrium at Point A ($10$ unemployed, $80$ workers earning a $60\%$ wage share, $10$ owners earning a $40\%$ profit share) is mapped onto a **Lorenz curve**, and explain how the increase in product-market competition from **part (d)** shifts the Lorenz curve and affects the **Gini coefficient**.
rubricChecks: a-b) Define ILO labour force, upward-sloping WS mechanism, and why firms refuse wage cuts below Point A
c) Contrast union bargaining (WS up) vs. voice (WS down) and explain Norwegian frontfag restraint (N* up, w* unchanged)
d) Show markup drop (0.40 -> 0.30) shifts PS up from 60 to 70, raising both w* and N*
e) Map kinks (10%, 0%) and (90%, 60%) on Lorenz curve and show inward shift reducing Gini
hints: Distinguish factors that shift the upward-sloping WS curve (effort/benefits/coordination) from factors that shift the horizontal PS curve ($\lambda$, markup $\sigma$).

Watch out for the classic trap: Coordinated Norwegian frontfag restraint shifts WS down (raising employment $N^*$, not $w^*$), whereas stronger product competition shifts PS up (raising $w^*$ and lowering Gini).
questions.solutionMarkdown:
- **a) Labour Force & Upward-Sloping WS Curve**:
  - The **labour force** consists of all working-age individuals who are either **employed** or **unemployed** (without work, available to start within 2 weeks, and actively seeking work during the last 4 weeks). It excludes economically inactive groups such as full-time students, retirees, disability recipients, and stay-at-home parents.
  - The **WS curve slopes upward** because as aggregate employment $N$ increases (moving right), the unemployment rate $u$ falls. With fewer unemployed people competing for vacancies, a dismissed worker can find a new job much faster. This reduces the expected duration of unemployment, raises the worker's reservation wage, and **reduces the cost of job loss (employment rent)**. To prevent shirking and motivate effort, employers must offer a higher real wage $w$.
- **b) Why Point A Is the Nash Equilibrium & Why Firms Do Not Cut Wages**:
  - At **Point A $(N^*=80, w^*=60)$**, the real wage required to motivate workers to exert effort ($w^{WS} = 60$) equals the real wage resulting from firms' profit-maximizing price-setting ($w^{PS} = 60$). Neither workers/HR departments nor pricing departments have an incentive to change wages, prices, or employment.
  - Even though unemployed workers would gladly accept a job below $w^* = 60$, firms **will not cut wages below Point A** because paying less than $w^{WS}$ destroys the employment rent required to discipline existing workers—workers would shirk, reducing labour productivity and lowering firm profits.
- **c) Union Bargaining vs. Voice Effects & Norwegian *Frontfagsmodellen***:
  - **Bargaining (strike-threat) effect**: If a union uses its strike threat to demand a wage above the minimum no-shirking wage, the **WS curve shifts upward**. Firms respond to higher nominal wage costs by raising prices $P$ to protect their markup $\sigma$, leaving the equilibrium real wage unchanged at $w^* = 60$ while **reducing employment** ($N^* \downarrow, u^* \uparrow$).
  - **Voice (motivation) effect**: When constructive union–employer dialogue improves working conditions and makes workers feel respected, the disutility of effort falls, **shifting the WS curve downward** and **increasing employment** ($N^* \uparrow$).
  - **Norwegian *Frontfagsmodellen***: In Norway, wage negotiations start in the internationally exposed export manufacturing sector (*frontfaget*), which sets a binding norm for the sheltered and public sectors. Because coordinated confederations (LO/NHO) internalize the macroeconomic threat of losing export competitiveness and causing unemployment, they exercise wage restraint—illustrated as a **downward shift of the WS curve**. Because $w^*$ is fixed by the horizontal PS curve, coordination does **not** directly yield a higher real wage; instead, it achieves **higher equilibrium employment and lower structural unemployment**.
- **d) Effect of Stronger Product-Market Competition ($\sigma: 0.40 \to 0.30$)**:
  - Stronger competition reduces firms' market power and lowers their profit markup $\sigma$ from $0.40$ to $0.30$. Firms charge lower prices $P$ relative to nominal wages $W$, which **shifts the horizontal PS curve upward** from $w_1^{PS} = 100(1 - 0.40) = 60$ to $w_2^{PS} = 100(1 - 0.30) = \mathbf{70}$ (while the WS curve is unchanged).
  - The economy moves up and right along $WS_0$ to a new equilibrium $E_2$: **both the equilibrium real wage ($60 \to 70$) and equilibrium employment ($80 \to 82.9$) increase**, while unemployment falls ($10 \to 7.1$).
- **e) Mapping to the Lorenz Curve & Gini Inequality**:
  - Ordering the $100$ individuals from poorest to richest, the baseline Lorenz curve starts at $(0,0)$, stays flat along the horizontal axis to **Kink 1 at $(10\%, 0\%)$** (the $10$ unemployed with zero market income), rises linearly across the $80$ employed workers to **Kink 2 at $(90\%, 60\%)$** (since the first $90\%$ of the population earns the $60\%$ wage share), and rises steeply across the $10$ owners to $(100\%, 100\%)$.
  - When stronger competition shifts the PS curve up in **part (d)**, unemployment falls from $10$ to $7.1$ (**Kink 1 shifts left to $(7.1\%, 0\%)$**) and the wage share rises from $60\%$ to $70\%$ (**Kink 2 shifts vertically up to $(90\%, 70\%)$**). The entire Lorenz curve shifts **inward toward the $45^\circ$ line of perfect equality**, shrinking Area $A$ and **reducing the Gini coefficient $G = A/(A+B)$ (lower income inequality)**.
questions.pitfall: Coordinated Norwegian frontfag restraint shifts WS down (raising employment $N^*$, not $w^*$), whereas stronger product competition shifts PS up (raising $w^*$ and lowering Gini).

questions.title: Exam-Calibrated Q12 · Competitive Market Equilibrium, Surplus & Cost/Tariff Shock (`Lecture 11 Prob. 2` + `V2026 Part 3` Synthesis
questions.promptMarkdown:
Consider a competitive market for artisan coffee beans where individual roasters are price-takers. At the initial market equilibrium $E_0$, the equilibrium price is $P_0 = 200\text{ NOK/kg}$ and the equilibrium quantity is $Q_0 = 50,000\text{ kg/week}$. The maximum Willingness to Pay on the linear demand curve $D$ is $P_{\max}^D = 400\text{ NOK/kg}$, and the minimum marginal cost on the linear market supply curve $S_0$ is $P_{\min}^S = 100\text{ NOK/kg}$.
- **a)** Explain what it means that roasters are **price-takers**, and explain why each roaster chooses to produce the quantity where $P = MC$.
- **b)** Calculate **Consumer Surplus ($CS$)**, **Producer Surplus ($PS$)**, and **Total Surplus ($TS$)** at $E_0$, and explain why $E_0$ is **Pareto efficient**.
- **c)** What is the marginal cost of the $50,000\text{th}$ kilogram of coffee before any tax? Suppose a new $20\%$ import tariff on raw green coffee beans increases every roaster's marginal cost by $20\%$ at every output level. What is the new marginal cost of supplying $Q_0 = 50,000\text{ kg}$, and how will roasters react if the market price temporarily remains at $200\text{ NOK/kg}$?
- **d)** Explain how the $20\%$ cost increase shifts the curves in the supply-and-demand diagram and establishes a new equilibrium $E_1 (Q_1, P_1)$.
- **e)** Will the new equilibrium price $P_1$ be equal to, higher than, or lower than $240\text{ NOK/kg}$? Explain your answer and state how the steepness (price elasticity) of the demand curve affects the size of the price increase.
rubricChecks: a) Explain price-taking behaviour and profit maximization at P = MC
b) Compute CS = 5,000,000, PS = 2,500,000, TS = 7,500,000 NOK/week and explain Pareto efficiency
c-d) Show tariff raises MC(50,000) from 200 to 240 NOK/kg, shifting supply up/left to E1
e) Explain why 200 < P1 < 240 (P1 = 225) and why steeper demand yields a larger price jump
hints: Check whether the shock changes buyers' WTP (shifts Demand), sellers' marginal cost (shifts Supply), or merely moves along an unchanged curve.

Watch out for the classic trap: A 20% marginal-cost tariff shifts supply vertically to $1.20\,MC_0$, but equilibrium price rises by strictly less than 20% ($200 < P_1 < 240$) because quantity falls along downward-sloping demand.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
- **a) Price-Taking Behaviour & $P = MC$ Rule**:
  - Because many small roasters sell a homogeneous product alongside many buyers, no single roaster can influence the market price $P_0 = 200\text{ NOK/kg}$—each takes $P_0$ as given.
  - If $P > MC(q)$, roasting one additional kilogram adds $P$ to revenue and only $MC$ to cost, increasing profit by $P - MC > 0$. If $P < MC(q)$, the last kilogram costs more to produce than it sells for, reducing profit. Profit is therefore maximized where **$P = MC(q)$**, making the upward-sloping $MC$ curve the firm's (and market's) supply curve.
- **b) Surplus Calculations & Pareto Efficiency**:
  $$\begin{aligned}
  CS &= \frac{1}{2} \times 50,000 \times (400 - 200) = \mathbf{5,000,000\text{ NOK/week}} \\
  PS &= \frac{1}{2} \times 50,000 \times (200 - 100) = \mathbf{2,500,000\text{ NOK/week}} \\
  TS &= CS + PS = \mathbf{7,500,000\text{ NOK/week}}
  \end{aligned}$$
  $E_0$ is **Pareto efficient** because all potential trades where a buyer's $\text{WTP} \ge \text{seller's } MC$ are carried out (up to $Q_0 = 50,000$), maximizing Total Surplus with zero Deadweight Loss ($DWL = 0$).
- **c) Marginal Cost at $Q_0 = 50,000$ Before and After the $20\%$ Tariff**:
  - Since $P_0 = MC_0(Q_0)$ at competitive equilibrium, the marginal cost of the $50,000\text{th}$ kg before the tariff is **$200\text{ NOK/kg}$**.
  - A $20\%$ cost increase raises the marginal cost at $Q_0 = 50,000$ to $200 \times 1.20 = \mathbf{240\text{ NOK/kg}}$.
  - If the market price stays at $200\text{ NOK/kg}$, then $MC_1 = 240 > P_0 = 200$: roasters lose money on the marginal kilograms and **reduce quantity supplied**.
- **d) Curve Shift & New Equilibrium $E_1$**:
  - The $20\%$ increase in marginal cost shifts the **market supply curve upward/leftward** from $S_0$ to $S_1 = 1.20\,MC_0$ (while the demand curve $D$ does not shift). At the old price $P_0 = 200$, excess demand emerges, bidding the price up and moving consumers up and left along $D$ until a new equilibrium $E_1(Q_1, P_1)$ is reached with **lower quantity ($Q_1 < 50,000$)** and **higher price ($P_1 > 200$)**.
- **e) Why $P_1 < 240\text{ NOK/kg}$ & Role of Demand Steepness**:
  - The new equilibrium price $P_1$ will be **strictly lower than $240\text{ NOK/kg}$** ($200 < P_1 < 240$). Because the demand curve slopes downward, consumers reduce their quantity demanded as price rises ($Q_1 < 50,000$). Because the supply ($MC$) curve slopes upward, producing a smaller quantity $Q_1$ lowers marginal cost along $S_1$ below $240\text{ NOK/kg}$. (With the exact linear curves $P^D = 400 - 0.004Q$ and $P^{S_1} = 120 + 0.0024Q$, $P_1 = \mathbf{225\text{ NOK/kg}}$ and $Q_1 = \mathbf{43,750\text{ kg}}$.)
  - **Steepness rule**: The **steeper (less price-elastic)** the demand curve, the less quantity demanded falls and the **closer $P_1$ rises toward the full $240\text{ NOK/kg}$**.
questions.pitfall: A 20% marginal-cost tariff shifts supply vertically to $1.20\,MC_0$, but equilibrium price rises by strictly less than 20% ($200 < P_1 < 240$) because quantity falls along downward-sloping demand.
